title: Anthropic
summary: Problems whose patterns are commonly reported in Anthropic coding interviews, from Easy to Hard. Approximate and hand curated, not an official or verified question list.
lesson:
About this list
- Each problem practices a pattern that candidates commonly describe from Anthropic engineering interviews: stateful in-memory data structures (filesystems, caches, versioned snapshots, hash tables), task and worker scheduling, rate limiting, dependency resolution, parsing, and graph traversal.
- Problems are grouped Easy, Medium, and Hard so you can warm up before practicing multi-operation APIs, versioned state, and concurrency-adjacent scheduling patterns.
- The selection is approximate. Interview loops differ across research, infrastructure, and product teams, so treat this track as systems-flavored coding practice rather than a prediction of what you will be asked.

What to expect
- Candidates often report progressive, engineering-focused coding rounds where you design and evolve an in-memory system across multiple stages—adding snapshots, TTL/eviction, dependency ordering, or throughput limits.
- Clean invariants, avoiding unnecessary copies (for example per-key version histories instead of full snapshots), and clear failure/edge-case behavior are commonly valued.
- Interviewers frequently ask how your in-memory design would scale under concurrency, high write rates, or bounded memory.

How to prepare
- Write down your data-structure invariants and operation complexities before coding, especially for multi-method classes.
- Favor incremental state updates and indexed lookups (binary search, heaps, doubly linked lists) over full scans or copies.
- After passing, think through how you would make the API thread-safe, persistent, or bounded in memory.
